title: Don't Look Up
synopsis: You found the comet. You also have to do a morning show. The comet does not care about ratings. Neither, soon, will you.

nodes.text: Your grad student's calculation matches yours. The math is not subtle. A six-mile-wide comet will, in 188 days, end most of the species. You sit very still.

choices.text: Call NASA before anyone else
Call your sister, just to say it out loud

nodes.text: Three days later you are in a beige conference room in Washington. The Chief of Staff eats a power bar while you brief. The President's daughter, in passing, asks if you've seen her hair.

choices.text: Demand a direct meeting with the President
Brief the science adviser thoroughly first

nodes.text: Your university PR has booked you on a morning show. The host wants you to be 'fun.' You bring three slides. He shows you two of them upside down.

choices.text: Be respectful and try to be heard
Lose your composure on air
choices.consequence: Sometimes anger is the only signal.

nodes.text: A tech billionaire named Peter offers a plan: rare metals on the comet, deflection by his company's untested rockets. He has a song. He has a TED Talk on the song. He has lawyers.

choices.text: Refuse and demand a public mission
Engage him cautiously to slow the deal
choices.consequence: Inside the room can be subversion.

nodes.text: Your on-air anger goes viral. Within twelve hours you are a meme, a political target, and, briefly, a sex symbol. None of it solves the comet.

choices.text: Use the platform for science
Disappear from media and focus on the work

nodes.text: Your grad student starts taking a sedative. Your colleague at the university quietly resigns to go to a cabin. The dean asks, with a smile, whether you've considered 'softening' your tone.

choices.text: Refuse to soften
Soften enough to stay employed
choices.consequence: You can't do the work if you can't pay rent.

nodes.text: A NASA engineer whose name you've been told to forget mails you internal data showing the deflection mission has been quietly delayed for Peter's mining plan.

choices.text: Leak it to the press
Take it to a senator who will hold a hearing

nodes.text: You go on the road — town halls in red states, blue states, places that are mostly highway. The questions are good. The exhaustion is worse than the comet. You sleep on planes.

choices.text: Keep touring until the deflection date
Pause to rest with your family

nodes.text: Two networks carry it. Three news anchors call it 'partisan.' The senator who held the hearing is, you discover, fundraising off your testimony before it ends.

choices.text: Confront the senator on her tactics
Take the win — congressional record matters

nodes.text: A movement forms — students, scientists, retirees who remember Apollo. They wear plain shirts with one word: 'Look.' You meet them and feel, briefly, that this can still be won.

choices.text: Join the movement as a public face
Support quietly from the lab

nodes.text: Your daughter, twelve, asks if you'd like to go skating with her on Saturday. You realize you have not been skating with her in two years. The comet, somehow, has made Saturday more important, not less.

choices.text: Go skating
choices.consequence: Be present at the home you have.

choices.text: Reschedule for after the deflection date

nodes.text: Eight rockets, mostly American, some European, one Japanese. The viewing party in the desert is the saddest party you have ever attended. The launch is, by all measurements, successful.

choices.text: Trust the math you signed off on
Stay on alert for the abort signal

nodes.text: Peter's rockets, late and underperforming, fail to deflect adequately. He blames the math, the comet, the woke. The public, in a startling moment of clarity, blames Peter.

choices.text: Push for the backup public mission, faster
Begin preparing the public for impact in 60 days

nodes.text: The deflection looks like it worked. Then a second measurement shows a smaller fragment still on intercept — city-killer, not planet-killer. The whole math gets done again, in public.

choices.text: Push for evacuation of the projected zone
Push for a second, smaller deflection

nodes.text: Three weeks out, every dinner table in the country is, in a strange way, the same dinner table. Your family eats together. You hold your daughter's hand. You realize you have, in this terrible chapter, become a better parent.

choices.text: Stay home for the last weeks
Go on the road for one last week of public service

nodes.text: The zone is evacuated — imperfectly, raggedly, but mostly. The fragment hits the ocean, not a city. The wave is bad. The wave is not what it could have been.

choices.text: Help with the long recovery
choices.consequence: The work doesn't end with the impact.

choices.text: Step back and write a book about the politics of it
choices.consequence: Document so it can't happen again.

nodes.text: Whatever the math says, you and your family sit down together for the dinner that night. The wine is bad. The food is good. The conversation, briefly, is about a memory from a beach trip nobody had thought about in ten years. You laugh.

choices.text: Make this the meal
choices.consequence: Presence is the only honest verb.

choices.text: Make the morning a phone call to anyone you still owe one

nodes.text: You stand in a parking lot with a clipboard and a clipboard-grade coffee, walking a displaced family through their paperwork. You realize most of what you know about the universe is, today, less useful than this.

choices.text: Stay in the field for the long recovery
Move to the policy side after a year

nodes.text: Late at night in your office you write the chapter on Peter. It is, you discover, the chapter you needed to write for yourself. You decide whether to lead the book with it or bury it in an appendix.

choices.text: Lead with it; name the cost
Bury it; let the science breathe first

nodes.text: Everyone else is asleep. You boil water you don't really need. The kettle whines. You decide whether tomorrow morning is a long meal at this table or a long list of voicemails.

choices.text: Make breakfast for whoever wakes first
Start the list of calls before sunrise

nodes.text: You spend the next decade on the politics of recovery, on the science of preparedness. You become a person who answers congressional phone calls. You age. You are tired. You are useful. That, in the end, is enough.

Your book is required reading in three different graduate programs ten years later. The next near-miss is handled with more sense, more speed, less Peter. You sign copies for students who were born after the night you stood on national TV and named the math.

Whatever the world does, you ate together. You held hands. You said the truth quietly. You realized, finally, that the meaningful answer to a comet is, has always been, presence with the people you love. The credits roll on a kitchen.

By morning you have called everyone you owed an apology to and everyone you owed a thank-you. The list is long. The voicemails are kind. Whatever happens next, you go into it as the person you tried, all your life, to become.
